title: --no-contracts
concept: The --no-contracts compiler flag strips all contract checks from the binary, delivering zero-overhead safety for release builds.
why: Contracts add runtime overhead. For production, you want the safety guarantees at compile time but zero cost at runtime.
theory:
## Stripping Contracts for Release

```sh
# Development build — contracts checked
xiom build app.xi

# Release build — contracts stripped
xiom build --no-contracts app.xi
```

### What Gets Stripped
- requires clauses — not checked at runtime
- ensures clauses — not checked at runtime
- Type invariant checks — not checked at runtime
- Contract violation reporting code

### What REMAINS
- The code itself (business logic)
- Explicit @llvm.trap() calls
- Explicit panic() calls
- Explicit assert() calls (unless also stripped)

### Performance Impact
```xiom
fn divide(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
  requires: b != 0;  // With --no-contracts: this check is REMOVED
{ return a / b; }
```

In debug: b != 0 is checked on every call.
In release: the check is gone — raw hardware division.

### The Trade-off
```
Development: Safety + Diagnostics (contracts active)
Production:  Speed + Size      (contracts stripped)
```
syntax_ref:
# Compile without contract checks:
xiom build --no-contracts main.xi

# The requires and ensures are removed from binary
tips: Use --no-contracts only when you trust your callers
Contracts are still valuable documentation even when stripped
Benchmark before and after --no-contracts to measure actual overhead
common_mistakes: Assuming --no-contracts means the program is unsafe — the type system still prevents many bugs
Forgetting that struct invariants are also stripped
Using --no-contracts without testing in debug mode first
